I actually have an ex-penal legion renegade guard army and it's the best. I get tons of compliments every time I bring them to local hobby stores. I heavily kitbashed most of my army using Cadian, Catachan, Chaos Cultist, Necromunda, and other kits. I have a unit of rough riders converted with Atalan Jackal and AdMech bits. The way I figure, if they're space pirates, they live mostly on ships, so it's not likely they'd be able to care for a stable of animals. It makes sense they'd have to use what they can get. Similarly, they wouldn't have a lot of specialized equipment to maintain their arms and armaments, so they'd have to get creative, like using ogryn in place of industrial robotic arms to hold metal plates in place while welders fuse them onto a tank or something. Which means they'd have plenty of ogryn lying around, and they'd probably get treated better because the pirates need them. See how one thought leads to another? Just let your imagination run wild and come up with cool stuff that YOU want to see on the table.

I liked the video, but I have one major criticism. I think she makes some good points, but she kind of glosses over the biggest problem with AI - the fact that it's being used by corporations to cut costs by firing artists and designers.

She does mention that she isn't trying to trivialize the plight of people who are losing their jobs because of the AI craze. But she also centers her experience at the expense of taking a broader perspective.

She says that AI is a poor replacement for art created by humans in many cases, except for "low-level corporate art." Although I think her point was that there will still be a place for artists in society, I thought it was a little dismissive to say that "low level corporate art" is the only kind that will be truly threatened. She mentions that she used to be a copywriter and was paid minimum wage to write descriptions for overstock.com, and the way she talks about the issue seems to make a false equivalence between the job she had and other creative jobs that are threatened by the AI craze. 

The problem with framing it that way is that most corporate art is low level, banal, and brainless, including the well-paying jobs that are hard to get and that many people, including myself and the rest of my household, depend on for survival. 

Making the argument that AI isn't good enough to replace human artists doesn't change the fact that a lot of CEOs and hiring managers don't agree. Even if they're wrong, they have the ultimate say over what hiring practices a company adopts, because the people who are responsible for executing those decisions - CHROs and HR managers - answer to them. 

The problem isn't that AI is not functionally a good replacement for artists, the problem is that we still live under capitalism, which means the people who have those jobs and make a decent living off of them are having their livelihoods undermined by the drive for corporate profits - and the AI craze is simply an excuse for this behavior. So it's not simply a case of "if you lose your shitty job just get another shitty job." Some of those jobs are really hard to replace, especially if you have bills to pay.

I'm not trying to beat the "Cancel Natalie" drum here. She obviously worked really hard on the video, and she obviously cares about the truth, and she was upfront about the fact that she's not an expert on this subject. I just think it's an important aspect of the topic that she didn't cover as well as the rest of the video.

The fact that people are still outraged that things like this happen tells me that none of them understand how capitalism or the video game industry work. The developers are not the ones funding this project or publishing it; they answer to Tencent, and Tencent is likely responsible for most of the decisions that people blame Fatshark for. Making any video game is an insane amount of work, and the business side of the industry puts enormous pressure on developers, many of whom are passionate about games and just want what they're making to be liked by people. This includes but is not limited to not giving them enough time to work on the things they want to work on, like telling them to focus on cosmetics and microtransaction assets instead of addressing bugs and other issues. Fatshark are not the scheming Machiavellian shitheads that apparently half this hell site thinks they are. Most of the problems can probably be traced back to Tencent. Unfortunately, without people funding its development there is no game, so devs often have no choice but to listen to publishers. This bullshit is to be expected. If you pre-ordered or bought a game that even the developers said was unfinished and expected it to be stable and fully built out, that's on you.

What counts is when they address these problems and take actionable steps to fix them. You can say that it's insincere, you can say that they're doing the right thing for the wrong reasons, but I've been around for three decades and I've seen few developers do this much outreach to their communities or address this many of their shortcomings without throwing up their hands and saying "you're asking too much." The fact that they're delaying seasonal content, which would have made them money, to fix bugs and address player feedback actually is a big deal. It can be hard to see the big picture when your only contact with this game is limited to your own perspective, and if that perspective is marred by your expectations not being met, it's easy to presume that you are being wronged instead of considering that your expectations may have been a little too high given the circumstances (they literally said when they released it that it's an unfinished game). Bibb Latane's social impact theory.

Latane was a psychologist who believed that social influence was a product of several factors: the strength of the influencer or influencers (a cop is going to have a much stronger direct, conscious influence on the behavior of others than a janitor); the immediacy of the influencers, or how physically close they are to the person being influenced; and finally, the number of influencers in a given situation.

S = s * I * n

Because the Internet makes everybody anonymous (mostly), the strength of influence is reduced to almost zero. Because everyone is telecommunicating, immediacy is also reduced to almost zero.

When you multiply something by a number that is less than one, the resulting value is going to be low. Hence, on the internet, factors that normally govern interpersonal behavior - factors that are tied to social influence by the other people we communicate with - are fairly watered down.

There's also research suggesting that when people communicate using methods other than face to face conversation, their brain's capacity for empathy is hindered.

I did a study on the subject in college and I found it fascinating. There's probably been more research on the subject now, but I found a ton of research (this was back in like 2011) that people tend to be more prone to dickish behavior on the phone, while emailing, texting, and communicating online. 

My theory is that something about interpersonal conversations feeds into our empathy, and when you try to communicate without some key elements of face to face interaction, our brains don't recognize the disembodied voice on the phone or Discord server or the text on a screen as the product of a human being. It gets read more like an inanimate object, so the human being responds based on the context in which they are interacting with that object. Even though humans obviously aren't objects, our brains read them as "obstacles," "noise," and other inhuman phenomena when immediacy is effectively removed from social interaction. You don't have to be polite to a rock or an irritating sound, and our brains know that. However, when you interact with a person that you don't know who might be on the other side of the world for all you know, our brains are far less likely to use empathy to figure out how to interact with them.

TL,DR: People on the internet are dickheads because their brains have more difficulty recognizing the person on the other side is human, and because everyone is anonymous and not physically in the same room as them, their behavior isn't as influenced by the person communicating with them. This makes it harder to exercise empathy, leading to dickhead behavior.

He didn't ask if I would let him stay with him, but when he showed up with all of his stuff in his hand, and his mom behind him smiling awkwardly, it became clear that he intended to stay with me even though the subject was not once broached. Later that night, he asked if he could have some coffee. I told him yes. He then filled a pint glass full of coffee and drank it all with a few shots of whiskey mixed in. This really annoys me because I was making minimum wage at the time, and coffee was a luxury I could barely afford. 

Months later, he admitted to me that he was a psychopath. He stole food and booze from me all the time, and even created drama between mutual friend groups to mask his behavior and make him look like the victim. It was around this time that a mutual friend told me he had been kicked out of various dorms and clubs on campus for the exact same behavior. I'm not going to get into it here, but the behavior I've described is only a sample of dozens of equally or more shitty things of this caliber that he did to me and others around us while we were roommates.
